title: Beef Bourguignon
subtitle: French braised beef with mushrooms and red wine
excerpt: Beef bourguignon is a slow Burgundian braise that turns a tough braising cut into something deeply tender and richly flavoured. It takes time, but almost all of that time is unattended in the oven. Make it the day before and it will be even better.
sourceNotes: Beef bourguignon is a Burgundian French braise that became famous internationally through Julia Child's writings. The long, slow cook in wine transforms tough braising cuts into something deeply tender.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Beef bourguignon is always better the next day. Make it a day ahead and reheat gently over a low heat.

content.text: Beef bourguignon has three key techniques that lift it above a standard beef stew. First, the beef is seared in batches until properly browned on all sides: this takes longer than most people allow, but it is where much of the flavour comes from. Second, the lardons are rendered first to release their fat before anything else goes in. Third, the braise is long and low, at a temperature where the liquid barely trembles.
Red wine is the traditional braising liquid: use a full bottle (750ml) of Burgundy or another robust red, and reduce the beef stock to 200ml. If you prefer not to use alcohol, use all beef stock.
The mushrooms go in during the last 30 minutes so they keep some texture. Serve with mashed potato, buttered egg noodles, or crusty bread.
Preheat the oven to 160C / 140C fan. Pat the beef cubes very dry with kitchen paper and season generously with salt and pepper. Dry beef browns; wet beef steams.

Set the large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the lardons without any oil and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has rendered and the lardons are lightly golden. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside, leaving the fat in the pan.

Increase the heat to high and add the sunflower oil. Working in batches of no more than 5 or 6 pieces at a time, sear the beef until deeply browned on all sides, about 3 to 4 minutes per batch. Do not crowd the pan. Remove each batch and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter to the pan, then the onion and carrot. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and tomato puree and cook for a further 2 minutes.

Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and stir to coat. Cook for 1 minute, then gradually pour in the wine (or stock if not using wine), scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Add the remaining stock, bay leaves and thyme. Return the beef and lardons to the pan. The liquid should just cover the beef; add a splash of water if needed.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and transfer to the oven. Cook for 2 hours. Remove the lid, add the mushrooms, stir gently, and return uncovered to the oven for a further 30 to 45 minutes until the beef is completely tender and the sauce has reduced to a glossy consistency.
Discard the bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve straight from the pan, or cool and refrigerate overnight and reheat gently on the hob the next day.

items.symptom: The beef is still tough after 2.5 hours
items.cause: The oven temperature was too high, or the cut was not well marbled.
items.fix: Return to the oven at a lower setting and check every 20 minutes. Beef chuck can take up to 3.5 hours at 160C. The meat is ready when it yields completely to a fork.

items.cause: The lid was on for too long, preventing reduction, or the flour was not cooked off properly.
items.fix: Lift the lid for the final 30 to 45 minutes, which is when the uncovered step reduces and concentrates the sauce. If it is still thin, transfer the beef to a warm dish, then simmer the sauce on the hob to reduce.

items.symptom: The beef is dry and stringy
items.cause: The braise overcooked, or the temperature was too high.
items.fix: There is limited rescue at this point. Stir the shredded beef back into the sauce with a good knob of butter to add richness.

items.cause: Insufficient browning of the beef or lardons at the start.
items.fix: A splash of Worcestershire sauce or a teaspoon of soy sauce can deepen the savouriness. For next time, sear in smaller batches and give each side a full 3 to 4 minutes.
